pending_items.title: How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
pending_items.content:
This week, the Geneva Convention held its Seventh Review Conference on the development of technological warfare and its humanitarian implications.

The review takes place every five years and aims to negotiate legally binding international agreements on restricting autonomous weapon systems, amid growing concerns over their use against civilians. However, powerful militarised countries like the US and Russia generally block progress.

Since the last review, the use of AI-powered weapons has accelerated exponentially, with much of the cutting-edge technology being used by Israelis against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by Israel .

Despite this, Palestine was barely mentioned during the UN meeting .

Last week, the Palestinian digital rights organisation 7amleh organised a conference in Brussels, attended by Middle East Eye, bringing together policymakers, journalists, politicians and researchers to assess the use of autonomous weapons in the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Nadim Nashif, 7amleh’s executive director, told the conference that Palestine is treated as a “laboratory” for AI, with technologies tested on Palestinians before being sold around the world and marketed as “battlefield-tested”.

Palestinians are among the most surveilled people on earth. Even before the genocide, he said, they were subjected to Israeli facial recognition and phone hacking, living in a “panopticon” of round-the-clock “mass surveillance”.

However, “what happened in Palestine does not stay in Palestine”, Nashif added, warning of the dangers of “having the power in the hands of a few people…controlling the future of humanity” without regulation or accountability.

“Gaza is a trial for these technologies,” Member of European Parliament (MEP) Benedetta Scuderi told the conference.

Scuderi argued that European defence agreements with Israel undermine international regulations.

“When technology comes in… humanity goes away,” she said, warning that “if we lose humanity then we are done”.

Scuderi referenced the European parliament’s recent screening of Israeli film NAZA , a documentary compiling interviews with Israeli army officials on the uses of these technologies in Gaza.

One soldier described feeling like he was in a “video game” when using technology such as Lavender , Gospel and Where’s Daddy to locate and target Palestinians.

European countries remain complicit through their involvement in production, research and arms sales to Israel, as exemptions allow European weapons to be exported despite their use in facilitating genocide, according to a 2025 UN report .

Scuderi called for human rights reviews of European budgets, acknowledging that even getting such measures “on paper” is difficult, with those in power viewing them as “an extra burden”.

Without regulation, she warned, technologies developed by western governments and used by Israel against Palestinians will inevitably be deployed domestically against journalists and activists, including in her home country of Italy. This phenomenon is known as the imperial boomerang .

Meanwhile, EU taxpayers continue to fund Israeli projects. In 2025, Israeli companies, universities and research institutes received €106m from the EU’s Horizon Europe fund.

At the conference, Harry Davies, a Guardian journalist and producer of NAZA , discussed a report he co-wrote with the documentary’s creator, Yuval Abraham, on Israel’s use of Microsoft cloud servers to store “a million calls an hour” made by Palestinians in the occupied territories.

In 2021, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella met the head of Israel’s military surveillance agency, Unit 8200, to arrange for vast amounts of data to be stored on Microsoft’s servers.

Following the investigation, Microsoft confirmed the findings and terminated its deal with the Israeli army, demonstrating the impact of journalism and public scrutiny.

While NAZA presents no new claims or information that Palestinians have not reported on for years, Davies said, it is “less about the actual technology than the people behind them, and the military systems” that enable the mass automated killing in Gaza.

In response , the Israeli army presented the technologies as mere tools, insisting decisions remain with military personnel.

The film shows “how meaningful that human involvement is”, Davies said, warning that relying on machine-generated statistical calculations can reinforce preconceived biases when operated in an atmosphere “of hatred and revenge”.

At the 7amleh conference, researchers from European Digital Rights revealed that 15 out of 27 European countries were discovered to have breached EU spyware regulations, with victims coming from civil society groups, journalists and political opponents.

In Spain, at least 65 individuals - including members of the European Parliament, Catalan presidents, legislators, jurists and members of civil society organisations - were allegedly targeted by the government using Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group. The government initially denied the allegations but later acknowledged spying on 18 individuals, citing national security concerns.

'Gaza is a trial for these technologies'

- Benedetta Scuderi, Member of European Parliament

In Poland, Pegasus spyware was used to target almost 600 people between 2017 and 2022 under the former Law and Justice government, “too many” of whom were targeted for being “inconvenient”, according to the current security services minister.

Following the scandal, the European Parliament launched the Pega committee in 2022 to investigate Pegasus and other spyware against civil society. However, its recommendations were never implemented.

Tech watchdog Citizen Lab found that a former MEP serving on the committee was hacked with Pegasus spyware at least three times during the investigation.

The European case in which an executive faced consequences was Greece’s 2022 spying scandal, known as “ Predatorgate ”, which came to light when opposition leader Nikos Androulakis discovered that his phone had been targeted with illegal spyware.

In February, a Greek court sentenced four people, including two Israelis, to prison, although an appeal remains pending.

One of the biggest obstacles to prosecution is gathering evidence, as defence and intelligence contracts are often highly classified. Another is the ability of transnational corporations to change jurisdictions to evade regulation.

Cases subsequently stall, with the EU failing to pursue them.

In 2017, Project Maven was launched by the US to accelerate AI military intelligence, using Google as a key contractor. But following public pressure, including from its own employees , Google terminated the contract and formulated ethical policies.

The contract was subsequently taken over by Palantir , which operated Maven during the US abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and the US bombing campaign against Iran. The latter included the “double-tap” strike on a girls’ school in Minab, which killed more than 170 people.

Palantir also holds a contract with the Israeli army, as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is deeply embedded in UK public services, including the National Health Service (NHS).

In 2020, US President Donald Trump pardoned the CEO of Israeli company Cellebrite for assisting cybercrimes, allowing the company to subsequently secure ICE contracts worth up to $96m.

Serbian police and intelligence forces used Cellebrite technology to extract data from phones belonging to journalists and activists.

In Russia and Kenya , the software was also used to target political opponents of the government.

Paragon Solutions, another Israeli company that supplies phone-hacking and listening devices, saw its $2m contract with ICE revived by Trump after former US President Joe Biden had paused it.

Paragon spyware was used to target European journalists and was investigated by Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee in 2025. The company, however, remains embedded in European markets, amid weak oversight and a reluctance to legislate and enforce regulations.

Technologies battle-tested in Gaza are increasingly used for state repression of migrants, left-wing journalists and politicians, and the Palestine solidarity movement.

EU leaders are at a “crossroads”, MEP Cecilia Strada told the conference, arguing that they can no longer feign ignorance about their role in facilitating crimes against humanity in Gaza or the use of European technologies to profit from mass slaughter.

The European Commission will review the EU-Israel trade agreement after a petition calling for its full suspension surpassed 1.1 million signatures from EU citizens this week.

In 2025, the European Commission proposed a partial suspension of the agreement, but member states failed to adopt the measure and are unlikely to do so now.

“The relationship with Israeli companies are not the fruit of political ties… they are the infested roots of those ties,” Strada said.

She pointed to Palantir’s lucrative UK contracts, describing them as not only “a threat to our democracies and fundamental rights, but also a fraud”, diverting public money away from public services and into private profit.

pending_items.title: The ‘eighth front’: Why Israel’s influence war in the US is failing
pending_items.content:
Israeli efforts to maintain the public goodwill of its principal ally, the United States, appear to be continuing despite a series of setbacks.

According to filings with the US Department of Justice’s Foreign Agent Registration Act on October 28, US influencing company Starboard was contracted by Israeli firm LDRS Group LLC, which declares itself as acting on behalf of the State of Israel to conduct “strategic communications and public relations services in the United States to promote the interests of the State of Israel”.

This builds on previous efforts to influence the US public. The Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft estimates that more than $1bn has been spent in direct funding for programmes to influence US public opinion in favour of Israel since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. That figure stands independent to the fundraising and political efforts of domestic organisations supporting Israel, such as the highly influential American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

US support for the multiple wars Israel has embarked on since the Hamas-led attack of 2023 has been close to unconditional. In addition to the annual grant, agreed under former President Barack Obama in 2016, the US has provided at least $25.5bn in appropriations and at least $21.7bn in military support, according to Brown University’s Costs of War project. Almost as critical has been the diplomatic support, which has seen the US use its veto t o block United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions as well as allowing Palestinian full UN membership.

However, evidence that US public support for Israel is collapsing is growing and has, for lawmakers in both countries, become unavoidable. Numerous polls point to growing hostility to Israel, especially among the young, stretching to include those on the right who hold Israel responsible for gulling President Donald Trump into an unwinnable war with Iran that is forcing their own cost of living, and gas prices, still higher.

President Donald Trump’s announcement that the US would end an Obama-era grant to Israel early, made on the day of the US midterms, was widely seen as an attempt to stave off the worst consequences of waning support for Israel across the political divide. But it did little to halt the rout that followed. The heavy spending by AIPAC and its affiliated organisations, estimated at $84m, in support of explicitly pro-Israel candidates, such as Senator Susan Collins of Maine, was largely considered a waste .

“The shift that has occurred in American public attitudes toward Israel is paradigmatic, generational, and lasting,” pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland’s Critical Issues Poll, said.

“You cannot unsee what you saw in Gaza, over three years. Israeli public relations campaigns are thus swimming against the tide. When they are visibly connected to Israel, they are even toxic, achieving the opposite results, as we have seen in the midterm elections.”

The pro-Israel campaigns are seeing the biggest impact among Republicans, especially among the Evangelical right. “But even there, there is evidence younger people are less impacted by these active and expensive campaigns,” Telhami said.

Concerns that Israel may be losing the battle for American hearts and minds reach beyond the state’s traditional allies on the right. Speaking with US media in May, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attributed the loss of US public support to unspecified foreign states’ manipulation of social media, ignoring the genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 70,000 people, including about 20,000 children, in the past three years. He characterised this as an “eighth front” in Israel’s ongoing wars with regional powers.

In March, Israel quadrupled the budget for its public diplomacy or “hasbara”, to $730m, much of it earmarked for US social media and American eyeballs. In November, it appeared to go further, bringing more than 250 of what Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs determined to be the next generation of US officials, journalists, influencers and community leaders to tour sites associated with the October 7 attack and cement relations with leading Israeli officials.

“Quadrupling the hasbara spend just means they’re more stupid than I thought they were and I already thought they were pretty stupid,” former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York Alon Pinkas said. “You change the conversation by changing the policy … So far, they haven’t let any foreign media into Gaza. Can you imagine what happens when they do? No amount of spending on their social media is going to mitigate what international journalists find there.”

Israel and its place in the Middle East had already been losing their relevance to the US before the war on Gaza, he said.

Washington had achieved energy security, the bogeyman of the USSR had been consigned to history, China had emerged as an area of critical interest, and both the public and politicians had grown weary of the kind of forever wars, he said, such as the current US-Israel war on Iran that shows no signs of ending.

“Add to that a resentful and angry president in the White House, and you have some idea of the job [potential incoming prime minister, [Gadi] Eisenkot or whoever, has ahead of them: One that no amount of Hasbara is really going to help.”

How far Israeli efforts to entrench US support among future leaders, or to game the country’s social media platforms, might go in reversing negative perceptions of Israel among the American public remains unclear. The midterm elections saw several of the country’s most vocal critics of Israel elected to Congress.

The prospect of renewed war with Iran, initiated through a partnership of two deeply unpopular leaders in the US and Israel, is unlikely to win hearts and minds.

“There’s no doubt that the three pillars of US support for Israel – the public, congressional, and the executive – are at an all-time low, certainly the lowest in my experience,” former State Department Middle East negotiator Aaron David Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment, said.

“It’s not just that we’ve seen the US engage in talks over Israel’s advice with Hamas, Yemen’s Houthi rebels and zeroing out aid [in] US weapons, but we’ve also seen a US president talk of his Israeli counterpart in extraordinary terms, and allowing highly critical phone calls of him discussing him to be leaked. However, this doesn’t mean we’re looking at a permanent rupture. A new Israeli government following different policies will take a good part of the tension out of public perceptions and Congressional angst.”
